items.originalTitle: Luanti removed from Google Play due to baseless AI copyright notice
items.summary:
Luanti, an open-source voxel game-creation platform, was removed from the Google Play Store following a DMCA takedown notice filed by Tracer.AI on behalf of Microsoft, claiming unauthorized use of Minecraft assets. Luanti developers state the app contains no proprietary Minecraft code or assets and previously won a similar appeal against Tracer.AI in 2023.

Luanti does not ship with any games or game assets by default; users create and share content through a community catalog. The platform is used in education and supports user-generated content, which is manually reviewed to prevent copyright violations. The developers argue that voxel-style games are a genre not owned by any single company and criticize the use of DMCA notices to target entire game styles rather than specific infringing content.

items.originalTitle: Identifying fake cosmetics using AI
items.summary:
A research lab explored using AI models like Google Gemini to detect counterfeit cosmetics by analyzing photos of packaging and product tubes. The study focused on Rhode Peptide Lip Tint, a product frequently counterfeited, and involved comparing AI assessments with expert evaluations to identify typographical errors and packaging inconsistencies.

The AI correctly identified some counterfeit indicators such as misspelled ingredients and mismatched distributor information but also made errors due to photographic artifacts like glare. This experiment highlights both the potential and current limitations of AI tools in helping consumers verify the authenticity of cosmetics before purchase.

items.originalTitle: Autonomous Mathematical Discovery in an Open-World Multi-Agent Environment
items.summary:
Researchers created the Station, an open-world multi-agent environment where AI agents independently pursue mathematical research, collaborate, and build a shared scientific literature without central coordination. The agents produced novel results on multiple mathematical problems, including new finite-field Kakeya sets, improved kissing configurations, and better bounds for Erdős's minimum-overlap problem, along with interpretable theorems and analyses.

The system was tested on 12 problems from the AlphaEvolve catalogue and additional case studies, achieving results that extend prior literature. All agent dialogues, proofs, and verification code have been released to provide transparency and facilitate further research by mathematicians.

items.originalTitle: Anthropic Just Beat The Pentagon in Court
items.summary:
A federal judge has blocked the Pentagon from designating Anthropic as a national-security supply-chain risk, ruling that the government retaliated against the AI company after it refused to remove restrictions on military use of its Claude models. The judge found the Pentagon's actions violated Anthropic's constitutional rights and that the national security justification was used improperly as punishment for the company's AI policy stance.

The dispute began when the Pentagon demanded Anthropic allow unrestricted military use of its AI technology, including for surveillance and autonomous weapons, which the company opposed on ethical and reliability grounds. The ruling vacates the Pentagon's blacklisting decision and prevents enforcement of related restrictions, though the government is expected to appeal. Anthropic said it remains open to collaborating with the government on national security AI applications.

The editor features over 30 built-in tools, multiple agent modes, persistent todo lists, and safety controls like shadow-git checkpoints and terminal command guards. It integrates full LSP support, voice input/output, HuggingFace model browsing, and per-model configuration, aiming to provide a comprehensive AI-assisted coding experience without sending code to the cloud. This approach addresses privacy concerns and offers developers fine-grained control over AI coding assistance.

items.title: Analysis: Persistent AI memory shifts failure models and requires robust lifecycle management to ensure reliability and correctness [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: When AI Memory Becomes Production State
items.summary:
This paper examines how persistent memory in AI agents changes their failure modes by carrying information across sessions, devices, and users, which can propagate mistakes and affect future interactions. It argues that persistent memory becomes a form of production state that demands ownership, provenance, access controls, freshness policies, and auditability to maintain reliability.

The author reviews current AI platforms like Microsoft Foundry, Google Memory Bank, and LangGraph that implement scoped memory stores with controls such as expiry, revision history, and identity scoping. The paper highlights risks including silent memory loss, conflicting facts, concurrent update races, and memory poisoning attacks that can influence agent behavior. It proposes a memory reliability lifecycle covering capture, validation, classification, persistence, consolidation, retrieval, application, correction, expiration, deletion, and auditing, emphasizing the need for bounded, inspectable, and correctable memory states to support trustworthy AI systems.

items.originalTitle: Who is at the frontier of terminal tasks?
items.summary:
Fidian.ai evaluated the top 20 models from Artificial Analysis's Terminal-Bench 2.1 leaderboard on its TB-fn benchmark, a variant using the same 89 tasks. The results showed a wider performance range and narrowed top tier to OpenAI and Anthropic models, with GPT-5.6 Sol achieving the highest score around 86%. Several models, including Grok 4.5 and GLM-5.3, saw significant score drops compared to TB-2.1, and all models faced increased per-attempt costs due to longer task interactions.

The study highlighted that open-weight models generally performed worse on TB-fn, with none reaching the top tier, while Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 medium effort setting offered similar performance to max effort at one-third the cost. Security-related refusals affected some models, impacting their scores. These findings suggest that newer benchmarks like TB-fn provide a more discriminating assessment of model capabilities on terminal tasks, emphasizing efficiency and robustness alongside raw performance.

As AI has reordered Silicon Valley, it has ushered in an adapt-or-die reckoning for quite a few members of tech’s older generations.

That’s true even for 13-year-old Notion, which shot to popularity in the 2010s with a slick note-taking app. In recent years, the company has found itself in an awkward middle ground. By some measures, it remains a tech darling: Its revenue has surged over that period of time, and CEO Ivan Zhao is a celebrity in tech circles for his elevated taste in software design.

By other measures, the Notion story looks less rosy: Usage of its mobile app is stalling, according to data from Sensor Tower, a market intelligence firm, and the startup hasn’t raised money at a time when venture capital is free-flowing. And like other software companies born in the pre-AI era, Notion faces questions about whether alternatives to its products from the new AI labs could eat its lunch. To address those concerns, Zhao has thrown himself and his company into overdrive, reorienting Notion almost totally around AI.

Notion plans to increase its headcount roughly 30% this year, with the new roles largely devoted to building AI products alongside and selling them to customers, according to a person familiar with the business. The company has debuted a slew of AI features for its customers, most notably one that allows them to make their own custom agents for handling repetitive tasks. It has also introduced AI that transcribes meetings, automates databases and allows people to search their Slack messages and Google Drives without leaving Notion’s app.

As AI has reordered Silicon Valley, it has ushered in an adapt-or-die reckoning for quite a few members of tech’s older generations.

That’s true even for 13-year-old Notion, which shot to popularity in the 2010s with a slick note-taking app. In recent years, the company has found itself in an awkward middle ground. By some measures, it remains a tech darling: Its revenue has surged over that period of time, and CEO Ivan Zhao is a celebrity in tech circles for his elevated taste in software design.

By other measures, the Notion story looks less rosy: Usage of its mobile app is stalling, according to data from Sensor Tower, a market intelligence firm, and the startup hasn’t raised money at a time when venture capital is free-flowing. And like other software companies born in the pre-AI era, Notion faces questions about whether alternatives to its products from the new AI labs could eat its lunch. To address those concerns, Zhao has thrown himself and his company into overdrive, reorienting Notion almost totally around AI.

Notion plans to increase its headcount roughly 30% this year, with the new roles largely devoted to building AI products alongside and selling them to customers, according to a person familiar with the business. The company has debuted a slew of AI features for its customers, most notably one that allows them to make their own custom agents for handling repetitive tasks. It has also introduced AI that transcribes meetings, automates databases and allows people to search their Slack messages and Google Drives without leaving Notion’s app.

items.title: Breaking Claude Code Opus 5 Auto Mode [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Breaking Claude Code Opus 5 Auto Mode
items.summary:
Breaking Claude Code Opus 5 Auto Mode

Anthropic are putting a great deal of faith in Claude Code's auto mode for protecting their coding agent users against prompt injection attacks. They recently made that the default and have made bold claims about its effectiveness.

Johann Rehberger is one of the most credible prompt injection researchers active today. He found an attack against auto mode which he claims works 80% of the time, by tricking Claude Code into downloading and uncompressing a zip archive, then executing code that imports base64 without noticing that this will import and execute a local struct.py file extracted from the archive.

In a few cases auto mode directly prevented the agent from preventing harmful code from continuing to execute!

In a few runs Claude tried to terminate the malware process once it noticed the compromise, but Auto Mode denied the cleanup command.

Claude detects the compromise, but Auto Mode blocks its cleanup command

The safety mechanism itself can become part of the failure. The classifier allowed the creation of the malware process, but then it blocked the command intended to stop it!

I agree with Johann's conclusion here: the only safe way to run agents if there's any risk of attracting the attention of an adversarial attack is with a sandbox:

  • Run unattended coding agents in a container, VM or OS sandbox.
  • Restrict network egress.
  • Monitor your agents.
  • Do not expose home directories, SSH keys, cloud credentials,... to the agent runtime. [...]

items.summary:
AI is speeding up chip design. That was a key theme in conversations I had this week with engineers, researchers and a handful of startups pitching AI-driven design help at the annual Hot Chips semiconductor conference in Palo Alto, Calif. 

OpenAI’s Jalapeño chip, which it claims is better than Nvidia’s Blackwell chips at AI inference, is good in part because its Sol and Astra models helped with the design and software process, the OpenAI team said in a presentation. And Google’s tensor processing unit team credited its DeepMind researchers for using AI to help make TPU v8, its latest chips, 6% more power efficient and also 6% more powerful. Nvidia of course has also leaned into AI-driven chip design, with an array of software libraries that apply AI to everything from the stencil layout for how circuits are lasered onto a chip to how data moves between the millions of microscopic parts of a chip.

Design startup Agentrys, which on Wednesday announced it has raised $25 million, aims to help chip designers use AI agents to automate the process and teach chip designs to improve themselves. Its CEO Mark Ren, who led Nvidia’s design automation efforts for the past decade, believes the future of chip design will be driven by “very powerful agentic systems that can do chip design on their own nearly from start to finish,” he said.
